gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 48,000 mAh bank holds only 6.7% more energy than a 40,000 mAh one (153.6 Wh vs 144 Wh, because its mAh are counted at 3.2 V), or works out per bank the Wh per pound (UGREEN 48K 42.7, Cuktech 30 57.8, AOHi Starship 40K 72.6), the dollars per Wh (UGREEN $0.77, AOHi $1.24 at store price) and the 126 Wh that Macworld's 1.8-charge test implies the UGREEN delivered.
standout_why: Compared against powerbanks.fyi (cited), Macworld's roundup and its UGREEN 48K review, and ChatGPT's own answer. powerbanks.fyi lists Wh, grams and price in separate columns for the UGREEN 48K and Cuktech 30 but computes no ratio, omits the AOHi Starship 40K and Techsmarter, and prices the UGREEN at $169.99 'checked on Aug 18'. Macworld gives '1.8 times' for a 14-inch M2 MacBook Pro but no delivered Wh, no Wh per pound and no cost per Wh. ChatGPT's answers give only generic estimates (100-125 Wh usable) and say they are not measured for the products shown. Tom's Guide (cited) could not be compared: the fetch returned only navigation (13,138 characters, no article body). The standout is 2 rather than 3 because the inputs are already on rival pages; only the arithmetic is new.
decides: It splits the pick rather than naming one winner. UGREEN 48K wins for a desk, car or campsite: it is the cheapest per Wh of the banks priced ($0.77 per rated Wh at $118.99) and the only one with a named laptop test (Macworld, 1.8 charges, about 126 Wh delivered). It does not win on capacity by the 20% its mAh label suggests, only 6.7%, and it weighs 3.6 lb. AOHi Starship 40K wins if the bank is carried: 72.6 Wh per lb against 42.7, about 1.6 lb lighter for 9.6 Wh less, at about $0.99 per Wh through our link. Cuktech 30 sits between them on weight (57.8 Wh/lb) but its maker's US store shows it unavailable today, so it cannot be the pick to buy. Both of ours place in the top three on these figures.

findings.label: Energy against a 40,000 mAh bank
findings.source_title: Ugreen 48000mAh Portable Power Bank review: more power and ports than most | Macworld
findings.note: Macworld: 'Battery capacity: 153.6Wh'. 153.6 Wh ÷ 48 Ah = 3.2 V per cell; 144 Wh ÷ 40 Ah = 3.6 V. 153.6 ÷ 144 = 1.067. At 3.6 V, 153.6 Wh is 42,667 mAh, so the label's 20% mAh lead is a 6.7% Wh lead.

findings.label: Wh per pound
findings.source_title: Ugreen 48000mAh Portable Power Bank review: more power and ports than most | Macworld
findings.note: 153.6 Wh ÷ 3.6 lb (Macworld: 'Weight: 3.6lb (1.65kg)') = 42.7. powerbanks.fyi lists 1,637 g, which gives 42.6.

findings.label: Energy delivered into a laptop (derived from Macworld's test)
findings.source_title: Ugreen 48000mAh Portable Power Bank review: more power and ports than most | Macworld
findings.note: Macworld: 'we recharged a 14-inch M2 MacBook Pro 1.8 times'. 1.8 × 70 Wh (Apple's stated battery) = 126 Wh; 126 ÷ 153.6 = 82%. This is energy landed in the laptop battery, so it includes the laptop's own charging loss.

findings.label: 14-inch MacBook Pro (2023, M2 Pro/Max) battery

findings.note: Input for the charge arithmetic. Ships with a 67 W or 96 W adapter, so a 100 W port covers it.

findings.note: Teoh Yi Chie (Parka Blogs) lists 144 Wh and 900 g; the review does not say the weight was measured. 900 g ÷ 453.6 = 1.98 lb; 144 ÷ 1.98 = 72.6. That is 1.7× the UGREEN 48K's 42.7 and about 1.6 lb lighter (3.6 − 1.98). Dealectric's record says 146 Wh, which gives 73.6.

findings.note: Parka Blogs gives a rated capacity of 24,000 mAh for USB devices; Dealectric's record says this is at 5 V. 24 Ah × 5 V = 120 Wh; 120 ÷ 144 = 83%. This is a rating at the USB port, before the laptop's charging loss, so it is not like-for-like with the UGREEN's 126 Wh. Parka Blogs reports no measured capacity.
